body.text: The United States yesterday announced a new tranche of sanctions against Cambodia’s Prince Holding Group, which it has accused of running a region-wide network of online scamming centers.

In a statement, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said that it had sanctioned an additional four individuals and 41 entities “that support the business network of Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization.”

“Prince Group TCO-affiliated actors have targeted victims in the United States and around the world through sophisticated cyber-enabled fraud schemes, including digital asset investment scams, romance scams, and other online financial fraud,” it stated. “Today’s action further targets the corporate and financial infrastructure that has enabled Prince Group TCO leaders to conceal assets, evade prior sanctions, and maintain access to the international financial system.” According to U.S. government estimates, such scams cost U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.

Treasury’s action comes after an operation in October of 2025, in which OFAC announced sanctions on 146 individuals and entities connected to Prince Holding Group, including its 38-year-old chairman Chen Zhi. It designated the group a “transnational criminal organization,” alleging its involvement in cyberfraud, human trafficking, and money laundering.

The sanctions were part of what Treasury described as the “largest action ever” to disrupt Southeast Asia’s scamming operations, which are run predominantly by Chinese criminal syndicates and have relied on a huge number of trafficked workers from across the globe. In a parallel announcement, federal prosecutors in the U.S. also unsealed an indictment charging Chen with wire fraud and money laundering. They accused him of “the construction, operation, and management of scam compounds reliant on human trafficking and modern-day slavery” and of authorizing bribes to foreign officials to protect his business interests.

Chen allegedly built his empire with the benefit of connections at the highest echelon of Cambodian politics. He served as an advisor to both former Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen and his son and successor Hun Manet, and was the recipient of the neak oknha title, one of the country’s highest honorifics. The sanctions, as well as growing pressure from Chinese authorities, in January prompted the Cambodian government to deport Chen to China, where he now faces a host of criminal charges, including some that carry the death penalty.
In June of this year, OFAC sanctioned an additional nine individuals and 26 entities linked to Prince Group, “including TCO leadership, investors in scam compounds, and front companies.”

According to OFAC, the individuals and entities named in the latest round of sanctions “have helped sustain Prince Group TCO’s illicit global operations after the October 2025 and June 2026 designations by managing offshore corporate structures, concealing beneficial ownership, facilitating commercial activities, and providing administrative and financial services to senior Prince Group TCO executives.”

They include Qiu Yong, whom Treasury described as a “key” member of the Prince network who controls multiple companies in Hong Kong and the British Virgin Islands, and who served as an employee of a company controlled by Chen Zhi, and his personal assistant Zhao Mengyao. Also listed were Cambodian nationals He Yujing and Visal Pang, who were sanctioned for holding property for, or co-directing companies with, Prince Group TCO executive Chen Bo, who was among those sanctioned in June.

More than 200 individuals and entities have now been sanctioned by the U.S. government, a testament to the intricacy of the networks established in order to conceal Prince Group’s ill-gotten profits. This also suggests that American investigators will be unraveling Chen’s tangled web for some time to come.
